newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil scandal won't slow reform voting - official.
newsitem.headline: Brazil scandal won't slow reform voting - official.

text.p: The Brazilian government is pressing ahead with voting on amendments to its civil service reform bill, despite a new corruption scandal which has rocked Congress, a government official said.

The government won three out of three votes on amendments to the bill in voting in the Chamber of Deputies late Tuesday and other proposed changes to the bill would be put to votes later Wednesday, the official said.

"It's not affecting us one bit," she said, when asked whether the government had noticed any change in its support in Congress following newspaper allegations five deputies took bribes to vote for a re-election bill earlier this year.
"The quorum (of deputies in the lower house) was high last night and it will be again today," the official said.

In voting on amendments Tuesday, the government maintained at 70 the age when public sector workers must retire. Opponents of the bill wanted to raise the age to 75. The government also defeated two other opposition amendments.

At least four further amendments were due to be voted in the Chamber of Deputies later today, including one which seeks to prevent state and municipal governments from setting their own caps on pay and pension.

The reform bill sets the monthly salary of a supreme court judge -- currently 10,800 reais ($10,188) -- as the maximum any public sector worker can earn, but allows local governments to set ceilings below that limit.
The article, which would help states and municipalities keep a grip on costs, is opposed by a powerful civil servants lobby.

However, the most controversial amendment to the bill -- a proposal that civil servants be allowed to keep their jobs-for-life guarantees -- would have to wait until next week before being put to a vote, the official said.

A central article of the reform would allow federal, state and municipal governments who spend more than 60 percent of their receipts on payrolls to dismiss workers whose jobs are currently protected by the constitution.
An opposition amendment would strike down that article and is reported to have support from members of parties allied to the government.
